title: Postpartum haemorrhage
blurb: Define and anticipate postpartum haemorrhage, take the NICE immediate actions, choose the right uterotonic and add tranexamic acid (NG235, RCOG GTG 52).
question: Chloe, para 1, chose a physiological third stage on a birth centre. Twenty minutes after the birth, with the placenta still in place, she has lost 750 mL and is still bleeding. What should the midwife do?

teach.h: What counts as a postpartum haemorrhage
teach.body: Formally (RCOG GTG 52): primary postpartum haemorrhage (PPH) is blood loss of 500 mL or more within 24 hours of the birth. Minor PPH is 500-1,000 mL; major PPH is over 1,000 mL, divided into moderate (1,001-2,000 mL) and severe (over 2,000 mL). In plain English: half a litre or more in the first day is a PPH, and over a litre is an emergency that needs the whole team. After discharge, sudden or very heavy or increasing bleeding needs advice without delay (NG194 1.2.4).

teach.h: Primary PPH by estimated blood loss
teach.caption: Continuously assess blood loss and the woman's condition, not just the measured volume (NG235 1.10.33).

teach.h: Antenatal risk factors: advise birth in an obstetric unit (NG235 1.10.29)

Detail
rows: Accreta spectrum; low-lying placenta; APH or abruption
Pre-eclampsia; Hb under 85 g/L at labour onset; BMI over 35
teach.caption: Highlight risk factors in the notes and agree a third-stage care plan with her (1.10.32).

teach.h: Risk factors that arise in labour (NG235 1.10.30-1.10.31)
items: Induction or augmentation with oxytocin or prostaglandins; oxytocin use in labour.
Prolonged first or second stage; precipitate labour.
Forceps, ventouse or caesarean birth; shoulder dystocia.
Delay in delivery of the placenta.
SSRI or SNRI antidepressants in the month before birth (small increased risk).

teach.caption: Ergometrine is contraindicated in pre-eclampsia, eclampsia, severe hypertension and severe cardiac, hepatic or renal disease.

Empty the uterus of retained tissue and repair any trauma.

teach.h: Worked scenario: Chloe on the birth centre
teach.body: Chloe is bleeding with the placenta in place after a physiological third stage, so NICE advises changing to active management. The midwife calls for help and arranges transfer to obstetric-led care, empties the bladder, rubs up a contraction and gives oxytocin plus ergometrine IM (she has no contraindication and has had no uterotonic), sites IV access and fluids, and uses controlled cord traction once the placenta separates. A second midwife records times, drugs and measured loss.

teach.text: The first-line drug depends on what she has already had: after oxytocin plus ergometrine, go to carboprost (or an oxytocin infusion), not more ergometrine in hospital. Tranexamic acid is ADDED to uterotonics; it does not make the uterus contract. And no manual removal of the placenta without an anaesthetic.

items: Primary PPH: 500 mL or more within 24 hours; major over 1,000 mL.
Antenatal risk factors (previous PPH, accreta, pre-eclampsia, Hb under 85, BMI over 35, para 4+): obstetric unit.
Immediate: call for help, empty bladder, massage, uterotonic, IV fluids, CCT, oxygen, transfer.
Choose the uterotonic by what was given in the third stage; add tranexamic acid 1 g IV.
Still bleeding: coagulation testing, blood products, EUA, repair trauma, balloon tamponade.

summary: You can now define and classify PPH, spot the women at risk, and take NICE's immediate actions in the right order. You can also choose the correct first-line uterotonic for each situation and add tranexamic acid.

A.q: After a vaginal birth, Erin's blood loss is measured at 1,300 mL. How is this classified under RCOG GTG 52?
A.why: Major PPH is over 1,000 mL; moderate is 1,001-2,000 mL and severe over 2,000 mL (GTG 52).

whyNot.0: 1,300 mL exceeds the minor range of 500-1,000 mL.
whyNot.2: Severe major PPH is over 2,000 mL.
whyNot.3: Secondary PPH occurs after the first 24 hours; this is within 24 hours of birth.

A.q: At a 36-week appointment, which finding means NICE advises birth in an obstetric unit because of PPH risk?
options: BMI of 30 at the booking appointment
Hb under 85 g/L at onset of labour
Second baby after a normal first birth
A.why: NG235 1.10.29 lists maternal haemoglobin below 85 g/L at onset of labour as a risk factor for which birth in an obstetric unit is advised.

whyNot.0: 110 g/L is above the 85 g/L threshold.
whyNot.1: The listed BMI risk factor is over 35.
whyNot.3: Grand multiparity (parity 4 or more) is the risk factor, not a second baby.

A.q: A woman is bleeding heavily after birth. Which is one of the immediate actions NICE recommends?
options: Empty the bladder and massage the uterus
Give oral iron and recheck in an hour
Start manual removal of the placenta at once
Lie her flat and wait for the doctor
A.why: NG235 1.10.33: call for help and give immediate treatment: empty the bladder, uterine massage, uterotonics, IV fluids and CCT if the placenta is undelivered.

whyNot.1: Oral iron treats anaemia later; it is not emergency treatment.
whyNot.2: NICE advises against manual removal of the placenta without an anaesthetic (NG235 1.10.28).
whyNot.3: Waiting passively delays treatment; immediate measures start at once.

B.q: Sana had a physiological third stage and no uterotonic. She now has a PPH from atony and no contraindications. What is the first-line uterotonic?
B.why: NG235 table 12: after physiological management, give oxytocin plus ergometrine IM (carboprost if contraindicated) or an oxytocin infusion.

whyNot.0: Carboprost is used here when ergometrine is contraindicated.
whyNot.1: Table 12 lists misoprostol among further treatments after the first-line drugs.
whyNot.2: Tranexamic acid is added to uterotonics, not used instead.

B.q: On the labour ward, Mei received oxytocin plus ergometrine for the third stage. She now has a PPH from atony. Which first-line drug does NICE suggest?
B.why: NG235 table 12: after oxytocin plus ergometrine prophylaxis, give carboprost IM or an oxytocin infusion.

whyNot.0: Ergometrine has already been given; the next step is carboprost or an oxytocin infusion.
whyNot.2: Repeating ergometrine is for when other drugs are unavailable, such as at home.
whyNot.3: Table 12 lists misoprostol among further treatments, not before carboprost or an infusion.

B.q: A woman with a PPH has had uterotonics. What does NICE NG235 recommend adding?
options: Vitamin K 10 mg by slow IV
Tranexamic acid 1 g orally, repeated at 6 hours
Tranexamic acid 1 g IV over 10 minutes
B.why: NG235 1.10.35: in addition to uterotonics, give tranexamic acid 1 g IV over 10 minutes, repeated after at least 30 minutes if bleeding continues.

whyNot.0: Vitamin K does not treat obstetric haemorrhage.
whyNot.1: The PPH dose is given intravenously, not orally.
whyNot.3: Calcium gluconate is the antidote to magnesium toxicity, not a PPH treatment.

C.q: Chloe chose a physiological third stage on a birth centre. Twenty minutes after the birth the placenta is still in place, she has lost 750 mL and bleeding continues. What is the best plan?
options: Call for help, massage, uterotonic, CCT
Await the placenta for up to 60 minutes
Manual removal of the placenta by the midwife
Give TXA, then wait 30 minutes to reassess
C.why: NICE advises changing to active management if there is haemorrhage (1.10.17) and, for PPH, calling for help, massage, uterotonics, IV fluids and CCT if the placenta is undelivered (1.10.33), with transfer to obstetric-led care.

whyNot.1: Haemorrhage is a reason to change to active management now, not to wait.
whyNot.2: Manual removal needs an anaesthetic and an obstetrician.
whyNot.3: Tranexamic acid supports, but does not replace, uterotonics and immediate measures.

C.q: At an antenatal review, which medicine history does NICE say gives a small increased risk of PPH?
options: Labetalol taken throughout the whole pregnancy
Sertraline taken in the month before birth
Folic acid 5 mg in the first trimester
C.why: NG235 1.10.31: SSRI or SNRI antidepressants in the month before birth may give a small increased risk of PPH, to be included in the bleeding risk assessment.

whyNot.0: Labetalol is not listed as a PPH risk factor.
whyNot.2: High-dose folic acid does not increase PPH risk.
whyNot.3: Vitamin D supplements do not increase PPH risk.

C.q: Bleeding continues despite uterotonics and tranexamic acid. The placenta is complete, there is no trauma and the uterus is atonic. Which next step does NICE list before surgery?
C.why: NG235 1.10.37: continuing PPH management includes intrauterine balloon tamponade before surgery, with coagulation testing and blood products.

whyNot.0: Repeated IV boluses are not the listed escalation; an oxytocin infusion is used.
whyNot.1: Fundal pressure is not a NICE PPH treatment.
whyNot.2: Ongoing haemorrhage needs active escalation, not expectant management.

reteach.title: Call, rub, drug, find
reteach.question: If you remembered only four verbs at a PPH, which four would keep the woman safe?

blocks.body: Call: get help early, including 999 at home. Rub: empty the bladder and massage the uterus to make it contract. Drug: give the right uterotonic for what she has already had, with IV fluids and tranexamic acid. Find: look for the source (tone, trauma, tissue, thrombin) while a colleague measures loss, records times and supports her and her companions.

root.label: PPH from atony
root.sub: what did she have in the third stage?

blocks.text: An oxytocin infusion is an option at every step, and carboprost replaces ergometrine whenever ergometrine is contraindicated.

explain.body: Primary PPH: 500 mL or more within 24 hours of birth. Minor 500-1,000 mL; major over 1,000 mL (GTG 52).

test.q: Primary PPH is blood loss of at least how much within 24 hours of birth?
test.why: RCOG GTG 52: primary PPH is the loss of 500 mL or more within 24 hours of the birth.

whyNot.0: 300 mL is below the PPH threshold.
whyNot.1: 750 mL is a minor PPH, but the threshold is 500 mL.
whyNot.3: 1,000 mL is the threshold for major PPH, not PPH itself.

explain.body: NG235 1.10.30: induction or augmentation, prolonged labour, sepsis, oxytocin use, precipitate labour, forceps or ventouse, caesarean birth, shoulder dystocia and delayed placenta all raise PPH risk.

test.q: Which event in labour is listed by NICE as a risk factor for PPH?
test.why: NG235 1.10.30 includes shoulder dystocia among intrapartum risk factors for PPH.

whyNot.2: An intact perineum is not a risk factor.
whyNot.3: Cephalic presentation is normal and not a risk factor.

explain.body: NICE suggests considering supplementary oxygen starting at 15 L/min through a non-rebreathing mask with a reservoir bag, aiming for saturations of 94-98%, and allocating a team member to support the woman and her companions (NG235 1.10.33, 1.10.36).

test.q: During a PPH, how should supplementary oxygen be started, according to NICE?
options: 4 L/min via a simple face mask
test.why: NG235 1.10.33: consider oxygen starting at 15 L/min via a non-rebreathing mask with reservoir bag, targeting 94-98%.

whyNot.0: Low-flow nasal oxygen is not the NICE starting dose.
whyNot.2: 4 L/min via a simple mask is below the recommended start.
whyNot.3: Waiting for severe desaturation delays oxygen; the target is 94-98%.

explain.body: Give tranexamic acid 1 g IV over 10 minutes alongside uterotonics, and repeat it after at least 30 minutes if bleeding continues (NG235 1.10.35).

test.q: If bleeding continues, when can tranexamic acid be repeated?
test.why: NG235 1.10.35: repeat tranexamic acid if necessary after at least 30 minutes for continuing PPH.

whyNot.0: 15 minutes is too soon; the minimum interval is 30 minutes.
whyNot.1: Waiting 6 hours is far too long in an ongoing haemorrhage.
whyNot.2: A 24-hour gap does not fit acute PPH management.
